ai.definition: A stellarator is a type of fusion reactor that uses a complex arrangement of 3D magnetic coils to confine plasma in a steady state without the disruptions seen in tokamaks.
ai.howItWorks: By employing a twisted magnetic configuration, stellarators generate a stable and continuous magnetic field that confines plasma. This design avoids the need for active stabilization systems used in tokamaks, making it potentially more reliable but also harder to build and maintain.
ai.problemSolved: Stellarators aim to overcome the limitation of tokamaks by providing a steady-state confinement without the disruptions that can cause energy loss and limit operational time.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process for stellarators is highly complex due to the intricate design requirements. It involves precise engineering and assembly of multiple magnetic coils, which must be perfectly aligned to achieve the desired magnetic field configuration.
ai.buildProcess: Construction begins with detailed simulations and modeling to ensure the magnetic fields are correctly configured. The magnetic coils are then precisely manufactured and installed in a toroidal geometry to create the confinement field. Testing involves extensive validation of plasma behavior under various conditions.
ai.costDrivers: High costs are driven by the complexity of design, precision manufacturing requirements, and the need for advanced materials and cooling systems. Long-term maintenance is also costly due to the delicate nature of the magnetic fields and components.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook remains uncertain as current prototypes have yet to achieve steady-state operation at sufficient temperatures and densities to sustain fusion reactions over extended periods.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations for stellarators since they are still in the research phase. However, safety guidelines for plasma handling and magnetic field management will be crucial once commercialization approaches.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving stable confinement at high temperatures and densities, as well as managing the complexity of the magnetic system. Financial risks stem from the high initial investment and long development timelines.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain due to the current focus on research rather than commercial applications. If successful, future projects could become profitable through energy production but require significant funding and time.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely involve improving magnetic field designs, enhancing cooling systems, and integrating advanced materials to reduce costs and improve efficiency.

glossary.def: A state of matter consisting of ions and free electrons, often used in fusion reactors.
A type of fusion reactor that uses a toroidal plasma confined by magnetic fields.
A condition where the plasma is continuously confined without external intervention or disruptions.

subsystems.name: Magnetic field coils
subsystems.role: generate the twisted, nested magnetic surfaces that confine plasma without inducing a net current.

subsystems.name: Vacuum vessel and plasma-facing components
subsystems.role: maintain ultra-high vacuum and provide a shaped boundary that matches the twisted plasma.

subsystems.name: Heating systems
subsystems.role: raise the plasma to fusion temperatures without relying on current drive.

subsystems.name: Cryogenic system
subsystems.role: keep superconducting coils at a few kelvin so they carry current without resistance.

subsystems.name: Blanket and tritium breeding
subsystems.role: absorb fusion neutrons, breed new tritium fuel from lithium, and extract heat (future power plant).

subsystems.name: Power conversion
subsystems.role: turn blanket heat into electricity (future power plant).
parts: steam turbine or closed-cycle gas turbine

subsystems.name: Control and diagnostics
subsystems.role: measure plasma parameters and adjust heating and magnetic fields to hold a steady state.

buildSteps.title: Optimize the plasma and coil geometry
buildSteps.detail: Use computer codes to find a set of three-dimensional coil shapes that produce a stable, well-confined plasma with low transport losses.

buildSteps.title: Wind the superconducting coils
buildSteps.detail: Wind cable into precise non-planar shapes, vacuum-pressure impregnate with resin, and test each coil at cryogenic temperature.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the vacuum vessel
buildSteps.detail: Roll and weld steel plates into the complex torus shape, then machine ports for heating, diagnostics, and the divertor.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the magnet system
buildSteps.detail: Position coils around the vessel with sub-millimetre accuracy and bolt them into a massive support ring that resists magnetic forces.

buildSteps.title: Install plasma-facing components
buildSteps.detail: Fit the divertor targets and first-wall tiles to handle heat loads of several megawatts per square metre.

buildSteps.title: Cool down and commission
buildSteps.detail: Evacuate the vessel, cool magnets to superconducting temperature, and trace magnetic field lines with electron beams to verify the confining geometry.

buildSteps.title: Create and heat the first plasma
buildSteps.detail: Introduce hydrogen or deuterium gas and use electron cyclotron heating to ionize and raise the plasma above 100 million °C.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate steady-state operation
buildSteps.detail: Run for extended periods—tens of seconds to minutes in current devices—to show continuous confinement without disruptive instabilities.

buildSteps.title: Integrate blanket and power conversion
buildSteps.detail: For a power plant, add a breeding blanket to make tritium, extract heat, and drive a turbine to generate electricity.

prerequisites.why: current machines use niobium-titanium coils, but reactor-scale fields may need high-temperature superconductors that are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: Wendelstein 7-X in Germany and the Large Helical Device in Japan show optimized stellarator confinement and long-pulse operation.
pathway.unlocks: confidence that twisted magnetic fields can confine plasma without current-driven disruptions.

pathway.milestone: Design and build optimized stellarators using high-temperature superconducting coils to shrink size and cost.
pathway.unlocks: faster, cheaper experiments that can test reactor-relevant plasmas.

pathway.milestone: A stellarator that breeds its own tritium and runs continuously for days.
pathway.unlocks: proof that the fuel cycle and materials can close in a steady-state device.

pathway.milestone: A pilot stellarator power plant delivering electricity to a grid.
pathway.unlocks: a route to continuous baseload fusion power.
firm, low-carbon electricity with no long-lived radioactive waste from fuel.
